INTERESTS OF AMICI CURIAE
Amici curiae are research and advocacy
organizations that, and Illinois government officials
who, believe military -derived semiautomatic assault
rifles—among the most dangerous firearms
available—should be banned from civilian use.1
The Violence Policy Center  is a national non -
profit educational organization that conducts
research on firearm violence and provides
information and analysis to policymakers, journalists,
researchers, advocates, and the general public . The
Violence Policy Center examines the role of firearms
in the United States, analyzes trends and patterns in
firearm violence, and works to develop policies to
reduce gun-related deaths and injuries. The Violence
Policy Center conducts numerous fact -based studies
on a wide range of gun violence issues, which have
influenced federal and state policymaking on the
regulation of firearms. This work includes extensive
research regarding the development, use, and
regulation of semiautomatic assault rifles.
The Lake County State’s Attorney’s Office, which
is run by Lake County State’s Attorney Eric Rinehart,
represents the residents of Lake County in criminal
and civil matters. The Office is also responsible for
long-term crime prevention planning and supporting
the victims and survivors of crimes. Finally, the Office
prosecuted Robert Crimo III for his July 4, 2022, use
of an AR -15 style rifle to kill seven individuals and

injure 48 others during a parade in Highland Park,
Illinois. The Office joins this brief out of a concern for
the safety of the residents of Lake County who may
suffer direct injury or vicarious trauma from the use
of assault weapons.
Amicus curiae the City of Highland Park, Illinois,
is a home rule municipality with a longstanding
commitment to public safety and reducing gun
violence. In 2013, the City adopted an ordinance
restricting assault weapons and large -capacity
magazines, modeled after the Cook County ordinance
at issue in this case. Highland Park successfully
defended its ordinance in Friedman v. City of
Highland Park , with the Seventh Circuit Court of
Appeals upholding the ordinance and the United
States Supreme Court subsequently declining to
review that decision. On July 4, 2022, Highland Park
experienced an unthinkable mass shooting during its
Independence Day para de, taking seven lives,
injuring 48 others, and forever changing the
community. The City's legislative history, experience
defending its ordinance, and firsthand experience
with gun violence give it a significant interest in the
outcome of this case and th e authority of local
governments to enact reasonable firearm regulations.
The Alvin H. Baum Family Fund strives to better
the lives of those who live and work predominantly in
the Chicagoland area. Through innovative grants and
collaborations, the Fund helps ignite new ideas and
promote solutions to ensure healthier, more
equitable, and peaceful communities. In addition to
making grants, through using its voice and influence,
the Baum Fund works to decrease gun violence in
northern Illinois.

3

The Illinois Alliance to Prevent Gun Violence
(IAPGV) is a coalition of grassroots organizations
from across Illinois working to reduce and prevent
gun violence. Recognizing that there is no easy
solution to the epidemic of gun violence that plagues
Illinois and the entire country, it is  resolute in its
determination to defeat this scourge at every level.
The IAPGV helped lead the grassroots organizing
effort in support of the Protect Illinois Communities
Act, making Illinois the ninth state in the country to
ban assault weapons. The IAPGV joins this brief out
of concern for  the devastation that assault weapons,
high-capacity magazines, and switches have brought
to communities across the state, from Highland Park
to Garfield Park to Rockford to East St. Louis and
everywhere in between.
Kids Above All is a nonprofit organization based
in Chicago that provides early childhood education,
safe and supportive housing, and trauma -informed
counseling for children and families who have
experienced trauma, including gun violence, poverty,
and homelessness.
The RIFL Coalition consists of over 60 national
and Illinois organizations, representing physicians,
survivors, advocates, and community leaders, all
standing together in pursuit of financial
accountability for the gun industry. The
Responsibility in Firearms Legislation (RIFL) Act
would require gun manufacturers to pay for a portion
of the direct public costs of firearm injuries. Members
from the RIFL Coalition meet regularly with
stakeholders and lawmakers to educate them on the
public safety and financial merits of holding the gun
industry accountable for the more than $800 million

4

of annual direct public costs currently burdening
Illinois residents.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
In New York State Rifle & Pistol Association, Inc.
v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022), this Court announced the
principle that government s seeking to regulate
firearms must show that a proposed regulation “is
consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of
firearms regulation. ” Id. at 24.  The Court also
emphasized that “the Second Amendment protects
the possession and use of weapons that are ‘in
common use ’” for civilian self -defense. Id. at 21
(quoting District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570,
627 (2008) ). And the Court noted an important
guardrail: Prohibitions on “the carrying of ‘dangerous
and unusual weapons’” are a significant —and
constitutionally permissible —part of the American
tradition. Ibid. (quoting Heller, 554 U.S. at 627).
These consolidated cases are about state and local
laws that regulate some of the most dangerous
weapons available to American civilians.  The Cook
County and Connecticut prohibitions on AR-15s and
similar semiautomatic rifles  adhere to the Second
Amendment because they bar a type of weapon whose
origin, features, and functionality reflect the purpose
these weapons were designed for—arming soldiers on
the battlefield. Semiautomatic assault rifles, like fully
automatic military assault weapons, are designed to
eliminate as many enemies as possible, as quickly as
possible, without the need for accuracy in
marksmanship. But w eapons designed for the
battlefield are now regularly used as a tool to
indiscriminately kill or maim American civilians at

5

home, work, school, houses of worship, grocery stores,
restaurants, and  practically anywhere else. 2 These
weapons emerged during the mid -twentieth century,
and thus represent precisely the type  of “dramatic
technological change[]” that this Court stressed
requires a “nuanced approach.” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27.
This brief proceeds in two parts. First, we explore
the military origins of semiautomatic assault rifle s,
detailing how their features were designed to achieve
a singular goal: maximum lethality on the battlefield.
We explain why, as a result, Congress and the
Executive Branch have  always treated this class of
weapon as distinct because they are inherently ill -
suited to self -defense or recreation.  Second, we
explore the dire public-safety effect of semiautomatic
assault rifles—underscoring that they are unusually
dangerous weapons properly subject to regulation.
Cook County and the State of Connecticut have
chosen to protect their citizens from the harm posed
by semiautomatic assault rifles, which have no proper
place in civilian life. The Second Amendment is no bar
to those reasonable restrictions, and the Court should
affirm the decisions of the Second and Seventh
Circuits.
ARGUMENT
The regulations at issue in these cases were
enacted in response to  tragic circumstances.  In
Newtown, Connecticut, a  man walked into an
elementary school with a lawfully  purchased
Bushmaster XM15 -E2S semiautomatic assault rifle

2 See generally  Violence Policy Center , Mass Shootings in the
United States Involving Large Capacity Ammunition Magazines
(May 2026), https://perma.cc/343Q-JZZW.

6

and “fired 154 shots in less than five minutes,” killing
twenty children and six teachers.  JA255‒56. The
state responded by imposing  restrictions on assault
weapons—including assault rifles —and on highcapacity magazines.  JA256. Cook County ’s assault
weapons ban  was originally enacted in light of
evidence showing that “assault weapons were 20
times more likely to be used in the commission of a
crime than other kinds of weapons” and  that “there
was no legitimate sporting purpose for the military
style assault weapons being used on the streets.”
Wilson v. Cnty. of Cook , 968 N.E.2d 641, 645  (Ill.
2012). The ordinance was later re -named to honor
Blair Holt, a high school student who  died from
gunshot wounds while protecting his friend after a
gunman opened fire on a crowded city bus.3
The question presented in these cases is whether
the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee
the right to possess AR -15 platform and similar
semiautomatic rifles.  As this Court recognized in
Heller, the right to bear arms  under the Second
Amendment “is not unlimited.”  554 U.S. at 626 ‒27.
Indeed, “[f]rom Blackstone through the 19th -century
cases, commentators and courts routinely explained
that the right was not a right to keep and carry any
weapon whatsoever in any manner whatsoever and
for whatever purpose. ” United States v. Rahimi, 602
U.S. 680, 691 (2024). Accordingly, this Court’s Second
Amendment jurisprudence does not “suggest a law

3 Cook County Board Bans Assault Weapons, Toughens
Penalties, Cook County Government (July 17, 2013),
https://perma.cc/WP2R-BY96; Leah Hope, 10 years later, school
remembers teen Blair Holt who was shot on CTA bus , ABC7
News Chicago (May 10, 2017), https://perma.cc/9DX5-WLTS.

7

trapped in amber.”  Ibid. The government may
regulate guns in a manner “ consistent with the
principles that underpin our regulatory tradition.” Id.
at 692.
One such principle is that circumstances
“implicating unprecedented societal concerns or
dramatic technological changes may require a more
nuanced approach.”  Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27.  “The
regulatory challenges posed by firearms today are not
always the same as those that preoccupied the
Founders in 1791 or the Reconstruction generation in
1868.” Id.
Semiautomatic assault rifles are an invention of
the modern era, emerging out of necessity during the
military clashes of the  twentieth century. Their
design features allow one individual to achieve
maximum lethality over a wide killing field. But while
that may be useful in war, t his high level of lethality
poses grave risk to the American public in our day-today lives—as shown by the number of mass shootings
involving semiautomatic assault weapons and the
severity of the injuries to the victims  of such
shootings. Cook County and Connecticut’s efforts to
regulate them are constitutional.
I. Semiautomatic Assault Rifles  Were
Intended and Optimized for Military Use.
The s emiautomatic assault rifle is a relatively
new invention, dating back to the 1960s. It is a
civilian analogue of military weapons developed
during World War I, World War II, and the Korean
War. By the end of the Korean War, military planners
had concluded that, under battlefield conditions, the
volume of fire could matter more than precise
marksmanship. Military assault rifles , developed in

8

response to these battlefield experiences, combine low
recoil, portability, and the ability to deliver rapid fire
at intermediate ranges.
As military -derived rifles entered the civilian
market, the federal government repeatedly treated
them as distinct from traditional sporting firearms
and adopted measures intended to limit their
availability. Nonetheless, the gun industry heavily
marketed these weapons by emphasizing their
military pedigree and combat -oriented features.
Today, semiautomatic assault rifles marketed for
civilian use contain the same  military-optimized
features as their predecessors—to devastating effect.
A. Semiautomatic assault rifles marketed
to civilians are militaristic in design and
origin.
Military assault rifles trace their origin  to the
submachine gun, which was developed during World
War I . As trench warfare created a  bloody and
intractable stalemate, the submachine gun emerged
as a preferred weapon because it was compact, easy
to carry, and light enough to be fired from the
shoulder or the hip. 4 During World War II, the
German army sought to develop a compromise
solution between t he rapid-fire but short -range
submachine gun and the long-range but slow-to-fire
rifle. The result was the STG (“Sturmgewehr,” or
“storm gun” ) 44, dubbed “the father of all assault
rifles.”5

4 Violence Policy Center, Bullet Hoses: Semiautomatic Assault
Weapons, at 8 (May 2003), https://perma.cc/7UJA-2FDX.
5 Ibid.

9

Assault rifles then became the military weapon of
choice for intense battlefield combat. In the 1960s, the
U.S. Army  reviewed three million casualty reports
from World War I and World War II, as well as data
from the Korean War. Its review yielded a surprising
conclusion: Overall, “aimed fire did not seem to have
any more important role in creating casualties than
randomly fired shots.” 6 In other words,
“[m]arksmanship was not as important as volume.” 7
That was because , despite devoting extensive
resources to “train [ing] combat infantryman to be
marksmen, few were capable of firing effectively
beyond ranges of 200 to 300 meters in the heat of
battle.”8
As a result, the Army sought to develop a weapon
that had low recoil and could rapidly fire a large
number of bullets at mid-range. That weapon was the
Armalite (AR) 15, which the military rechristened as
the M-16 assault rifle.9
The M -16 saw extensive service during the
Army’s next major combat operation , the Vietnam
War. With the M -16 in hand,  the tactic of spray -
firing—or “spray and pray” —became common in the
battlefields of Vietnam.10 Soldiers could spray a large

7 Ibid.
8 Ibid.
9 Duncan Long, Assault Pistols, Rifles and Submachine Guns 57
(Paladin Press 1989).
10 Bullet Hoses, supra note 4, at 12.

number of bullets over a broad killing zone, without
having to aim at any individual target.11
Meanwhile, Colt Firearms Corporation bought
the manufacturing license for the AR -15 in 1959 and
began to market it to American civilians as the
semiautomatic AR-15 Sporter Rifle. 12 It replicated
many features of its military predecessor, including
its pistol grip, barrel design, and rear “finger
adjustable” sighting system.13
Other semiautomatic assault rifles followed a
similar developmental ar c, as gun manufacturers
adopted military-derived firearm designs for sale in
the civilian market. For example, the Ruger Mini-14
semiautomatic rifle  is a “scaled -down” version of a
military M-14 battle rifle.14 While it was sold only to
military and law -enforcement markets upon its
introduction in 1972, due to high demand  the
company introduced a “sporterized” semiautomatic
version aimed at civilians a few years later. 15 The
Smith & Wesson M&P [Military & Police] 15 assault
rifle, introduced in 2006, was “specifically designed to
satisfy the functionality and reliability needs of global
military, law enforcement, and security personnel” —

11 Violence Policy Center, Key Points About Assault Weapons
(2017), https://perma.cc/YM8W-GBYM.
12 Long, supra note 9, at 58.
13 Ibid.
14 Id. at 114.
15 Ibid.

11

but was also sold to civilians at sporting goods
stores.16
The common features of all these civilian-targeted
assault weapons are precisely what made them so
valuable to the military: Even a poor marksman can
indiscriminately kill shocking numbers of people with
these firearms, in a matter of seconds.
B. Congress has acted to regulate these
military-derived weapons.
Congress has long recognized that these types of
weapons belong primarily in the hands of the
military.
After World War II and subsequent conflicts,
increasing numbers of surplus military firearms
entered the United States. In 1955, domestic firearms
manufacturers produced the vast majority of rifles
available in the U nited States —only 15,000 rifles
were imported that year.17 But by 1966, 500,000 rifles
were imported, and by 1968, over one million rifles
were imported .18 These imported weapons were
“largely military surplus.”19
In 1968, Congress took action to keep this tidal
wave of military implements out of civilian hands —
all the while emphasizing why these weapons had no
place in civilian life.  The Gun Control Act of 1968

M&P15 Semiautomatic Assault Rifle  (February 2018),
https://perma.cc/9S46-B25D.
17 Franklin Zimring, Firearms and Federal Law: The Gun

18 Ibid.
19 Ibid.

prohibited the importation of “surplus military
firearms” and all other guns unless the Secretary of
the Treasury certified them as “ particularly suitable
for sporting purposes.” 18 U.S.C. § 925(d)(3).20
During the legislative debate  on the 1968 law ,
members of Congress emphasized the danger that
military weapons posed to American civilians. As the
bill’s primary House sponsor, Representative
Emanuel Celler, remarked, “[t]he clear objective of
these import restrictions is to arrest the present flood
of imports of surplus military weaponry  and low -
priced foreign -made firearms generally, since these
types of weapons have caused major law enforcement
problems.”21 And Senator Thomas Dodd, the Act’s
primary Senate sponsor, stressed that the United
States was “the only country in the world that allowed
military surplus weapons to be sold to its citizens.”22
Notably, the Gun Control Act was passed in the
wake of the assassination of President Kennedy:
“When Congress passed the [Gun Control Act], it was
well known that the rifle used to assassinate
President John F. Kennedy was a surplus Italian
military rifle imported into the United States.”23
In the years that followed  the enactment of the
Gun Control Act, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and

21 114 Cong. Rec. 21784 (1968).
22 114 Cong. Rec. 27462 (1968).
23 Dep’ts of Justice & Treasury, Gun Violence Reduction:
National Integrated Firearms Violence Reduction Strategy ,

Firearms was tasked with determining which
shotguns and rifles had legitimate sporting purposes.
It concluded that weapons designed for military and
law enforcement use were not “suitable for traditional
sporting purposes, such as huntin g, and trap and
skeet shooting,” and therefore could not be
imported.24
The 1968 Act was not the last time Congress
treated semiautomatic assault weapons as a distinct
class of firearm. In 1994, Congress enacted the Public
Safety and Recreational Firearms Use Protection
Act,25 more popularly known as the Federal Assault
Weapons Ban.  That Act banned the production of
certain semiautomatic assault weapons and  of highcapacity ammunition magazines that held more than
ten rounds.
The Federal Assault Weapons Ban  sunset in
2004. At least one scholarly study found that  the
number of mass shootings declined during the decade
that the federal ban was in place —and rose “sharply
upward” in the decade-plus after it lapsed.26
These federal regulations of military assault rifles
and their civilian analogues underscore that the
federal government has understood, from the outset,

1989) (ATF Report), https://perma.cc/VHZ3-2V92.
25 Pub. L. 103-322, Title XI, Subtitle A.
26 John Donohue & Theodora Boulouta, That Assault Weapon
Ban? It Really Did Work , N.Y. Times (Sept. 4, 2019),
https://perma.cc/T9YE-CKBL; see also John Donohue, The

the new and  unusual danger such weapons pose to
civilian life in the United States.
C. Gun manufacturers have long
advertised the military pedigree of
semiautomatic assault weapons.
Gun manufacturers have long emphasized the
military pedigree of these weapons in their marketing
to civilians. During the floor debate on the 1968 Gun
Control Act, Representative Fred Schwengel spoke
out against the availability of mail-order guns and the
manner in which they were marketed to discontented
civilians. As he explained, “t he very advertising of
many of these mail -order fir earms seems geared to
attracting the attention of the power -hungry
individual, the crank, the thrill -seeking youngster,
and the like. Neither the type of weapons sold nor the
pitch of the advertising is aimed for the serious
sportsman, the gun collector, or the avid target
shooter.”27
Representative Schwengel specifically noted
advertisements for semiautomatic rifles  that
included:
For $99.50, a special antitank gun ideal
for long-range shots at deer and bear or
at cars and trucks. 28
and:

27 114 Cong. Rec. 21784 (1968).
28 114 Cong. Rec. 21812 (1968) (emphasis added).

15

Get your N.K.V.D. secret police pistol of
the type that fanatic Russian agents use
to terrify and kill enemies of the state.29
According to Representative Schwengel , “ [i]t is not
the responsible gun enthusiast and sportsman who is
the target of this advertising ”—but rather the “man
with a feeling of insecurity or inferiority ,” “the
impressionable juvenile ,” “the deranged individual
who misguidedly seeks to protect himself, others, or
society by taking the life or lives of another.”30
While the precise firearms discussed in the 1968
debate are not exactly the same  semiautomatic
assault rifles regulated by the laws at issue here, the
debate nonetheless documents the long-running
practice of using military terminology, foreign-conflict
imagery, and anti -personnel associations to market
firearms to civilian consumers.
Indeed, the gun industry’s militarized messaging
continues today. Bushmaster—whose XM-15 assault
rifle was the murder weapon in the Sandy Hook
Elementary School tragedy —throughout its various
corporate iterations has regularly used military and
law-enforcement images in its advertisements. 31 Its
graphics have included  military or police -related
terminology, including “duty” and “patrol,” as well as
phrases like “Bravery on Duty.”32 The overall effect is

29 Ibid. (emphasis added).
30 Ibid.
31 See generally  Violence Policy Center, The Militarized
Marketing of Bushmaster Assault Rifles  (April 2018),
https://perma.cc/6X35-4EX4.
32 Ibid.

16

imagery and language that focus on the use of the
XM-15 rifle and similar weapons in “ offensive, antipersonnel situations and environments.”33
This marketing is clear counterevidence to the
industry claim that commercial prevalence alone
makes these rifles ordinary civilian arms. Widespread
ownership of these weapons cannot be divorced from
decades of marketing emphasiz ing military identity,
combat-derived functionality, and the connection
between civilian products and weapons designed for
military and law -enforcement use.  Manufacturers
themselves have treated military pedigree as a
principal selling point for these firearms, rather than
an incidental feature.
D. Modern semiautomatic assault rifles
have many features that are virtually
identical to military rifles.
Today’s semiautomatic assault rifles are virtually
identical in most respects to corresponding military
weapons, and permit an individual to spray a large
number of bullets within a short period of time. 34
Those key design features in common include the
ability to accept high-capacity magazines; rear pistol

II. Semiautomatic Assault Rifles Are
Dangerous and Unusual Weapons  Properly
Subject to Regulation.
The Second Amendment has never protected
weapons that are “dangerous and unusual.”  Bruen,
597 U.S. at 21; Heller, 554 U.S. at 627. Semiautomatic
assault rifles fall squarely within that category.  The
military-derived features described above —highcapacity detachable ammunition magazines, pistol

stocks—were designed to lay down “a high volume of

B. Semiautomatic a ssault rifles inflict
uniquely severe injuries.
Assault rifles are not only more likely to be used
to shoot many people; they are also more likely to
cause grievous harm to each person they hit. The AR-
15’s standard cartridge strikes with roughly 1,300
foot-pounds of muzzle energy —nearly four times the
energy of a typical 9mm round. 65 Trauma surgeons
“treating wounds from high-velocity rifle ammunition
describe tissue cavitation, organ disruption, and
vascular damage that bear little resemblance to
typical handgun injuries.” 66 Such wounds “cavitate
tissue, fracture bone at a distance from the track, and
damage vessels and organs the bullet never touches,”
making them “more resource -intensive to treat than
typical gunshot injuries.”67
The casualty data reflect that difference.
Excluding the 2017 Las Vegas shooting, mass
shootings in which an AR -15 was fired killed an
average of 10.1 people and wounded 13.7 —compared
with 6.0 killed and 4.8 wounded in shootings
involving no assault weapon. 68 And the harm does not

shooter to kill and maim more people, more quickly,
and more severely than would be possible with a
traditional firearm. Even when police respond almost
immediately, the toll can be staggering: In Dayton,
Ohio in 2019, officers killed a shooter within 32

26 people, killing nine.71
Weapons that have proven so uniquely suited to
mass killing —and that cause injuries of a different
kind than ordinary firearms—are precisely the sort of
“dangerous and unusual” weapons that legislatures
have long been free to regulate. The Cook County and
Connecticut laws fall comfortably within that
tradition.
